title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
summary: JSON is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format derived from ECMAScript. It defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data. This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON and was replaced by RFC 8259.

eli5.summary: JSON is a plain-text way to write lists and labeled values so different programs can share them. This version fixed mismatches and has since been replaced by RFC 8259.

subtitle: The text format that describes structured data with objects, arrays, strings, numbers and three literals, as it stood in 2014.

tldr.problem: JSON had become very widely used, but earlier specifications left room for patterns that caused interoperability problems and contained a few errata.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7159 restates the JSON grammar, lets any value be a JSON text, and adds guidance on duplicate names, number range, character encoding and string comparison.
tldr.outcome: It was obsoleted by RFC 8259, so it documents an intermediate version of the JSON specification.

today: RFC 7159 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8259, so use that for the current JSON specification. It obsoleted RFC 4627 and RFC 7158.

sections.title: What JSON Is and What Changed
sections.content:
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a text format for the serialization of structured data, derived from the object literals of JavaScript. It can represent four primitive types (strings, numbers, booleans and null) and two structured types (objects and arrays). Its design goals were to be minimal, portable, textual and a subset of JavaScript.

This document updates RFC 4627. Wide use had revealed patterns that were allowed but caused interoperability problems, and two errata had been reported. The goal here is to apply the errata, remove inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, and highlight risky practices. All the specifications of JSON syntax agree on the syntactic elements of the language.
sections.eli5: JSON is a plain-text way to write things like a shopping list or a labelled set of boxes. This update cleaned up places where people read the rules differently.

sections.title: Grammar, Values, Objects and Arrays
sections.content:
A JSON text is a serialized value. Earlier specifications limited a JSON text to an object or an array; this one allows any value. A value MUST be an object, array, number or string, or one of the literal names false, null and true, which MUST be lowercase. Six structural characters ([ ] { } : ,) may be surrounded by insignificant whitespace: space, tab, line feed and carriage return.

An object is curly brackets around zero or more name/value members, with a colon between name and value and commas between members. Names SHOULD be unique. If they are not, behavior is unpredictable: many implementations report only the last pair, others report an error, and some report all pairs. Parsing libraries also differ on whether member order is visible.

An array is square brackets around zero or more comma-separated values, and the values need not be of the same type.
sections.eli5: An object is a set of labelled boxes, an array is a numbered line of things, and you write them with curly and square brackets. If you give two boxes the same label, nobody knows which one you meant.

sections.title: Numbers and Strings
sections.content:
A number is written in base 10 with an optional minus sign, an integer part, and optional fraction and exponent parts. Leading zeros are not allowed, and values such as Infinity and NaN are not permitted. Implementations may set limits on range and precision. Software that uses IEEE 754 binary64 (double precision) is widely available, so a number such as 1E400 hints at an interoperability problem. Integers in the range from -(253)+1 to (253)-1 are interoperable, meaning implementations agree exactly on their values.

A string begins and ends with quotation marks. The quotation mark, the reverse solidus and the control characters U+0000 through U+001F must be escaped. Any character may be escaped as \uXXXX, and a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is written as a 12-character UTF-16 surrogate pair, for example \uD834\uDD1E for the G clef (U+1D11E). Short forms like \\ and \n exist for popular characters.
sections.eli5: Numbers are written the ordinary way, but very huge or very precise ones may get squashed by some programs. Words go in quotation marks, with a backslash for special characters.

sections.title: Encoding, Unicode and Comparison
sections.content:
JSON text SHALL be encoded in UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32. The default is UTF-8, which the most implementations read successfully. Implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark to the start of a JSON text, though parsers MAY ignore one.

The grammar allows strings that cannot encode Unicode characters, such as "\uDEAD", a single unpaired surrogate. This has been observed when a library truncates a UTF-16 string in the middle of a surrogate pair. Software that receives such values behaves unpredictably, and may report different string lengths or even crash.

For comparing member names, the RFC says to compare Unicode code units numerically. Comparing strings with escapes unconverted may wrongly conclude that "a\\b" and "a\u005Cb" are different.
sections.eli5: Programs should agree on how letters are stored as bytes, and should compare the real letters rather than the backslash codes used to write them.

sections.title: Parsers and Generators
sections.content:
A JSON parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar, and MAY accept non-JSON forms or extensions. It may set limits on text size, nesting depth, the range and precision of numbers, and the length and contents of strings. A JSON generator MUST produce text that strictly conforms to the grammar.

The practical rule is therefore to be strict in what you produce and to document any limits you apply when you read.
sections.eli5: When writing JSON, follow the rules exactly. When reading it, be prepared to accept all valid JSON, though you may refuse things that are too big.

sections.title: Security and the Media Type
sections.content:
JSON's syntax is borrowed from JavaScript, so it is possible to parse a JSON text with eval(). The RFC calls this generally an unacceptable security risk, because the text could contain executable code along with data declarations. The same applies to eval-like functions in any language where JSON texts conform to that language's syntax.

The IANA section registers the media type application/json, with file extension .json and no charset parameter, since adding one has no effect on compliant recipients.
sections.eli5: Never run a stranger's JSON as if it were a program. Read it as data only, or it might do something sneaky.
